title: Remark
body_md: If~${\mathcal{I}}$ contains all input directions and~${\mathcal{O}}$ all output directions present in~${F}$, then~${\partial_\mathcal{I}=\partial_\mathcal{O}}$, but costs may differ: Forward mode makes~${O(|\mathcal{I}|)}$ {\tt jvp} calls, reverse mode~${O(|\mathcal{O}|)}$ {\tt vjp} calls. If~${F}$ is scalar, for example, then~${|\mathcal{O}| = 1}$ and a single {\tt vjp} suffices, recovering the familiar reverse-mode advantage of standard {\tt jax.grad}.

title: Remark
body_md: Compositions of~${P}$,~${\partial_M}$, and~${\nabla_M}$ give rise to the standard objects of differential geometry on~${M}$ (intrinsic differential operators, Laplacians, and curvature tensors), with no Christoffel symbols, coordinate charts, or dimension-specific formulas required. A parallel integration theory pairs~${\partial_M}$ with the directed volume field~${\mathrm{d}X}$ (the tangent space~${I(x)}$ weighted by the Riemannian measure~${\lvert\mathrm{d}X\rvert(x)\in\mathbb{R}}$) to give a single multivector-valued fundamental theorem subsuming the classical Stokes-type results~\citep{Hestenes_Sobczyk_1984}. Appendix~\ref{sec:api_manifolds} develops these in full, showing the full `API' for differential geometry.

title: Remark
body_md: The condition that the $\{b^J\}$ span the same subspace as $\{b_J\}$ can be relaxed, but convolutes the proof slightly. As an example of such an instance, consider the conformal euclidean algebra $\Lambda(\mathbb{R}^{n+1,1})$ with basis $e_1, \ldots, e_n, e_+, e_-$, and then consider the change of basis $e_\infty = e_+ + e_-$ and $e_o = \frac12 (e_- - e_+)$. It is easy to verify that $\langle e_\infty, e_o \rangle = -1$, meaning that the reciprocal of $e_\infty$ is $-e_o$. We can thus see that any space $W$ containing $e_\infty$ components without the $e_o$ components will have a reciprocal space that is not contained within it.

name: Forward-mode proof

title: Proof
body_md:
Letting $\mathcal{O}$ index the output blades, so that $F(X) \in\operatorname{span}\{b_K: K\in \mathcal{O}\}$ for all $X$. Take $\mathcal{I}$ to be the corresponding input index set over which $X$ varies. Note that the adjoint is defined implicitly by the property $\langle C, dF_X[A] \rangle= \langle dF^\ast_X[C], A\rangle$ for the multivector inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$:
\begin{align}
    \partial_\mathcal{I} F &= \sum_{J\in\mathcal{I}} b^J dF_X[b_J] \\
    &= \sum_{J\in\mathcal{I}} b^J \left[ \sum_{K\in\mathcal{O}} \langle b^K, dF_X[b_J]\rangle b_K\right] \\
    &= \sum_{J\in\mathcal{I}} b^J \left[ \sum_{K\in\mathcal{O}} \langle dF_X^\ast[b^K], b_J\rangle b_K\right] \\
    &= \sum_{K\in\mathcal{O}} \left[ \sum_{J\in\mathcal{I}} \langle dF_X^\ast[b^K], b_J\rangle b^J \right] b_K \\
    &= \sum_{K\in\mathcal{O}} dF_X^\ast[b^K] b_K
\end{align}
and we are done as our metric aware $\texttt{vjp}_{\langle\cdot, \cdot \rangle}$ computes $dF^*$ with respect to the multivector inner product instead of the Euclidean one.

name: Reverse-mode proof

title: Remark
body_md: If we assume that $F$ varies over the basis index set $\mathcal{O}$, and takes inputs $X$ which vary over the basis index set $\mathcal{I}$, then computing the forward mode $\partial_{\mathcal{I}}$ requires $\lvert \mathcal{I} \rvert$ \texttt{jvp} calls and geometric products. Computing the reverse mode $\partial_\mathcal{O}$ requires $\lvert \mathcal{O} \rvert$ \texttt{vjp} calls and geometric products. This implies that for computing multivector derivatives of scalar functions is most efficient in reverse mode, while most vector derivatives are more efficient to compute with the forward mode form since they only require $n$ \texttt{jvp}'s.
